A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same authors, model, and task-ordering principles. Their main text, figures, equations, and Appendices A–C are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical simulations and image-classification experiments, including theoretical-versus-numerical comparisons in Figure 2 and classification results in Figures 5 and 7.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results using subsampled data to estimate task similarity and ordering in Figures 9–10.

M1.justification: The latent teacher-student model, periphery-to-core and max-path ordering rules, and zero-shot-transfer similarity estimator in Eq. 16 are retained. The new experiments apply the same procedures with smaller estimation datasets.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic tasks and Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 classification coverage, including the existing multiclass experiment. Figures 9–10 change sample availability within these datasets, without adding datasets, populations, or task requirements.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain periphery-to-core versus core-to-periphery, max-path versus min-path, and random ordering. Figures 9–10 reuse these comparator sets; the added application citations are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 9 adds similarity-estimation protocols using 0.1%, 1%, and 10% of CIFAR-10 training data alongside the existing full-data control. Figure 10 uses 1% across the three image datasets. Both source-task training and target-task transfer evaluation use subsamples; architectures, metrics, and five-epoch training remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantial sensitivity study addressing how much advance data task-order optimization requires. Figures 9–10 examine estimation-data fractions, robustness across the retained datasets, and ordering preferences at different task counts. v1 contains no corresponding analysis of sparse similarity-estimation data.

E5.justification: The existing standard-error reporting, random-seed information, and task-set/order averaging descriptions are retained. v2 introduces no new uncertainty estimator, repeated-run count, or significance-testing procedure. Its statements about significance of the new results do not specify a changed statistical method.

E6.justification: Figures 1–8 retain their findings, while Figures 9–10 add a substantial set of accuracy curves and ordering-preference ratios. Section 5.2 reports comparable ordering gains with 1% estimation data on CIFAR-10, non-significant gains at 0.1%, and weaker robustness on CIFAR-100. Figure 9g–h repeats Figure 7c–d, and Figure 10c–d repeats Figure 9c–d; these repeated panels are not new results.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 corrects the Hamiltonian-path length from a sum of input correlations to a sum of dissimilarities. Eq. 15 also corrects the distance indices and identifies the error contribution as delta-epsilon. The main theorems and appendix proofs otherwise retain their mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract and concluding theoretical contributions remain unchanged. The introduction adds the substantive claim that approximately 1% of the data can suffice to estimate task orders that significantly outperform random ordering.

C2.justification: v2 develops the practical argument for collecting pilot data before ordering subsequent acquisition and training. It adds qualifications concerning the 0.1% setting and negative-similarity CIFAR-100 results, and attributes weaker CIFAR-100 effects to fewer images per label. The original theoretical limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.4 documents the sparse-data implementation: train from random initialization for five epochs on the source-task subsample, evaluate transfer on a target-task training subsample, and apply Eq. 16. Existing architecture, optimizer, hardware, and source-code access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references by Verwimp et al., Kumari et al., Ibarz et al., and Zhu et al. to support application and impact discussions. Its positioning relative to Bell and Lawrence and Lin et al. is unchanged. Publication metadata updates for existing references do not introduce new works.

P1.justification: The introduction’s applicability discussion is expanded and reorganized, Section 5.2 gains a sparse-data discussion, and an Impact Statement is added. Local wording and the erroneous Figure 3 color reference are corrected. Most prose and the section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, substantially reflowing equations, captions, and figure placement. Figures 9–10 add multipanel displays, including explicitly identified repetitions of earlier panels. The existing figures retain their substantive visual content.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens practical relevance by testing whether task ordering remains useful with limited advance data, a question untested in v1. Figures 9–10 provide both supporting evidence and failure boundaries, Appendix C.4 explains the protocol, and Section 4.3 repairs mathematical inconsistencies. These are useful, focused improvements to an otherwise stable contribution; the original theoretical assumptions and application limitations remain.
